sources.summary: Valid continues Latin validus, directly derived from the base of valere. Health, strength and legal/logical efficacy are related senses.
English value comes through Anglo-French value/valu and valer from Latin valere. Its noun and denominal verb share this history.
French valeur continues late Latin valor, itself derived from valere.
Italian valido continues Latin validus, derived from valere.
Italian valere includes worth, efficacy, validity and sufficiency; vale is a finite form, not the English valley noun.
Technical valence develops through German Valenz/valentigkeit and Latin valentia. Chemical use precedes analogical linguistic use; the latter is documented in Tesniere in 1953.
Valenza continues late Latin valentia derived from valere. Chemical combining capacity and linguistic complement capacity are related technical senses.
French val continues Latin vallis. This valley noun is distinct from the valere worth/strength row.
English vale continues Anglo-French val from Latin valles/vallis; deeper origin is uncertain.
Valley continues Anglo-French valee/Old French valede, formed from val with a noun suffix. It belongs to the same valley lexical history.
Vallo1 continues Latin vallum, a palisade or fortification; transferred ditch/groove senses remain in that entry.
Vallo2 is a masculine variant of valle, influenced by apocopated val in place names; it also denotes an administrative district.

The editorial name entry records Valerius as a Roman family name related to valeo and lists national counterparts including Valeriy/Valerio. Its cited Lewis-Short source could not be directly retrieved; primary-source confirmation remains a blocker.
The municipal history independently documents Roman Valentia as the city preceding Valencia. This does not resolve every lowercased corpus occurrence or every place named Valentia.
Previously saved independent lexical control: cheval continues Latin caballus, not vallis or valere. Reuse the frozen route dossier evidence; no new route audit.
Italian stivale is a boot noun from Old French estival; its final val spelling does not establish valere or vallis.
The dictionary provides a native mental row with um, umnyj and derivatives. Local morphological coherence does not establish international formal continuity.
The dictionary separates kryl-o and lists animal and aircraft senses and derivatives. A wing component has a full kryl base, not lo.
The official orthographic dictionary lists antikrylo and plural antikrylja. The finite wing component analysis is a research inference alongside the krylo dictionary.
The dictionary gives singular amerikanec and genitive amerikanca. -ca contains stem alternation and case ending; it is not an associative root.
Pizza is an Italian loan noun. Cyrillic final ca transliteration does not relate it to the person-noun inflection pool.
The Russian encyclopedia identifies umlaut as the German term Umlaut for vowel alternation. Its initial um is distinct from Russian mental um.
Umyvat is the washing verb paired with umyt. The u + my lexical segmentation is a finite research analysis; initial um does not establish the mental row.
The publisher entry identifies atrium/atrij and Latin atrium as the architectural hall/court. The final Latin noun spelling is not Russian mental um.
Indexed dictionary text lists Russian val for an embankment, wave or shaft. Its spelling alone does not identify the international worth or valley row.
Frozen seven national heads and ten negative/withheld controls are reused with their independent sources and exact records; no repeated route audit.
